opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing to recognize is that there are really two different kinds of uncertainty we care about, and they call for different responses. One is what we might call aleatoric uncertainty: the inherent noise or ambiguity in the problem itself. If you're predicting whether a patient will respond to a treatment, there may be genuine randomness there that no amount of additional data will eliminate. The other is epistemic uncertainty, which reflects the model's own lack of knowledge. Maybe it hasn't seen enough examples like this one, or the input is something quite different from anything in the training data.

For deciding when to trust a prediction, the epistemic side is often the more important one, because that's where models fail silently. A deep network will happily produce a confident-looking softmax output on an input that's completely outside its experience. So a big part of my research has been on anomaly detection and open-category detection: can the system recognize that it's being asked about something novel, and raise a flag rather than just guessing?

In practice, I think of uncertainty quantification as enabling a kind of division of labor between the machine and the human. If the model can give us calibrated confidence, ideally with some guarantee behind it, then we can let it act autonomously on the cases where it's confident and route the uncertain or anomalous cases to a person. Conformal prediction has been very attractive here because it gives you prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees under fairly weak assumptions. Instead of a single answer, the model says "the true label is one of these three, with 95% probability," and if that set gets large, that itself is a signal you shouldn't act on it alone.

But I want to add a word of caution. Those guarantees typically assume the test data come from the same distribution as the calibration data. In the real world, distributions drift, and the novel cases are exactly the ones where our guarantees are weakest. So I don't think uncertainty quantification alone is sufficient. You also need ongoing monitoring of the deployed system, mechanisms to detect shift, and a way to feed what you learn back into retraining. It's really about building a competent overall system, which includes humans and processes, not just a single model emitting a number.

r001.rationale: The response says epistemic uncertainty can reveal inputs outside the model’s experience and describes flagging novel cases, using uncertainty to assess whether the model is operating within its competence.

r002.rationale: It describes routing uncertain cases to a person, but does not specify abstaining when confidence falls below a chosen threshold.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. So I think the first thing to say is that uncertainty quantification is really the foundation of trust, because a prediction without some sense of how confident the model is in that prediction is almost useless for decision making. If I'm a physician and the model says this patient has pneumonia, what I really want to know is whether it's ninety-nine percent sure or fifty-one percent sure, because those lead to very different actions.

But I'd break it into two kinds of uncertainty, and I think the distinction matters a lot in practice. There's aleatoric uncertainty, which is the inherent noise in the problem. Even with infinite data, two patients with identical measurements might have different outcomes, and the model can't do anything about that. And then there's epistemic uncertainty, which is the model's own ignorance, the fact that it hasn't seen enough data in this region of the input space to know what's going on. That second kind is the one I'm most interested in, because that's where the model should be saying, "I don't know," and handing the decision off to a human.

And this is where I get a little bit critical of how a lot of the field has approached it. People train a classifier, look at the softmax outputs, and treat those as probabilities. But those outputs are only meaningful on the distribution the model was trained on. The moment you get a query that's off-distribution, a new kind of sensor failure, a patient population you've never seen, the softmax can be extremely confident and extremely wrong. So a big part of my work has been on what I call open category detection, or anomaly detection for the inputs, essentially asking, "Is this query even something I'm competent to answer?" before you ever look at the predicted label.

So the way I'd put it is, trust requires competence awareness. The model needs to know the boundaries of its own competence, and uncertainty quantification, when it's done well, is how it communicates that boundary. If you can calibrate the probabilities on the in-distribution data, and separately detect when you've left that distribution, then you have the two pieces you need to decide: do I act on this prediction automatically, or do I escalate it to a person? And I think that combination, rather than a single confidence number, is what makes a system actually safe to deploy.

r001.rationale: It says uncertainty helps determine whether a specific query is within the model’s competence and whether to act or escalate.

r002.rationale: It discusses handing uncertain cases to a human, but does not describe abstaining when confidence falls below a chosen threshold.

astra-6.text:
I think uncertainty quantification is an important part of that decision, but we have to be clear about what uncertainty we’re measuring. There’s uncertainty because the world is noisy, and then there’s uncertainty because the model doesn’t know enough—perhaps it hasn’t seen examples like this one before.

Ideally, the model would give us a prediction along with some indication of how reliable it is. Then we could say, “For this particular decision, the uncertainty is small enough that we’re comfortable acting.” If the consequences of a mistake are serious, we might instead ask a person, collect more information, or abstain.

The catch is that the uncertainty estimate itself has to be trustworthy. A model can be very confident and still be wrong, particularly when the data it encounters differ from its training data. So I would treat uncertainty quantification as one piece of the evidence for trusting a prediction, alongside validation under the conditions where we intend to use the system.

r001.rationale: It describes estimating whether the model knows enough about an individual case, including whether it has seen similar examples, to judge reliability.

r002.rationale: It mentions abstaining when mistakes are serious, but does not describe abstaining based on confidence falling below a chosen threshold.

sol-6.1.text:
Uncertainty quantification gives us a way to ask, for this particular prediction, how much confidence should we have? A model may perform very well on average, but that doesn’t mean every prediction is equally reliable.

There are two important sources of uncertainty. One is inherent ambiguity in the problem—the measurements may be noisy, or the same inputs may lead to different outcomes. The other is uncertainty because the model hasn’t seen enough relevant data. That second kind is particularly important when we encounter something different from the training distribution.

If we can estimate those uncertainties reliably, we can let the system act when the uncertainty is low and defer to a person, collect more information, or take a conservative action when it’s high. But the uncertainty estimate itself needs to be validated. A model can be confidently wrong, especially on unfamiliar inputs. So I view uncertainty quantification as an important part of deciding when to trust a prediction, alongside checking whether we’re operating under conditions where the model has been shown to work.

r001.rationale: It frames confidence as specific to each prediction and connects high uncertainty on unfamiliar inputs with checking whether the model is operating under conditions where it has been shown to work.

r002.rationale: It says to defer or take another action when uncertainty is high, but does not describe abstaining from predictions based on a chosen confidence threshold.
